title: Databases
concept: A database keeps data safe across crashes and lets many clients read and change it at once. Most relational databases share the same core: a change is written to a log before it touches the data files, a commit is the moment that log record is safely on disk, and copies on other machines, called replicas, stay current by replaying the primary's log.

posts.title: Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL
posts.ageNote: A 2016 account of Postgres 9.2 and the MySQL of that time. It is here for fundamentals that are not tied to a version: what a write-ahead log is for, what physical and logical replication each ship to replicas, and why every index costs a write. The specific limits it describes may have changed in later Postgres and MySQL releases. The only fix the post itself confirms is that the 9.2 replication bug was fixed.

digest.problem: In 2016 Uber explained why it moved its core storage from Postgres 9.2 to MySQL. Every update cost several disk writes, replication sent too much data between its two sites, a Postgres bug left replicas with wrong data, replicas cancelled long-running queries, and each major version upgrade meant hours of downtime. The post is useful mostly for how carefully it explains what a database does underneath.
digest.constraints: Uber ran a primary with replicas on the US West Coast and disaster-recovery replicas on the East Coast, and bandwidth between them was expensive. Archiving the write-ahead log to a storage service could not keep up at peak. Postgres also struggled past a few hundred active connections, while application bugs sometimes left many transactions open and idle.

walkthrough.step: Rows are versions at an address
walkthrough.explanation: Postgres 9.2 stored each version of a row as an immutable tuple at a physical location called a ctid, and every index, including the primary key, pointed straight at that location.

walkthrough.step: An update writes a new version
walkthrough.explanation: Changing a row writes a new tuple at a new location, so every index needs a new entry pointing to it, even indexes on columns that did not change.
Every change to tuples and indexes is first written to the write-ahead log. After a crash, the database replays the log to repair its files and roll back work that was never committed.

The primary streams its log to replicas, which apply it like a never-ending crash recovery. The result is a byte-for-byte copy of the primary's disk, which ties every replica to the primary's exact layout and version.
A replica cannot keep old row versions for its own readers while applying log records that remove them, so a query that blocks replay for too long gets cancelled.

walkthrough.step: InnoDB points at the primary key
walkthrough.explanation: In MySQL's InnoDB, the primary key index holds the row itself, secondary indexes store the primary key, and old versions go to an undo area. An update touches only the indexes whose columns changed, at the cost of two lookups for a read through a secondary index.
MySQL's binary log records statements or row changes rather than disk pages, and each replica works out its own index changes.
Postgres leaned on the operating system's file cache and used a process per connection; InnoDB managed its own buffer pool and MySQL used a thread per connection.

tradeoffs.chosen: MySQL with InnoDB, often under Uber's own sharding layer, Schemaless.
tradeoffs.rejected: Keeping Postgres and working around it with cascading replication, connection poolers, and the pglogical extension for logical replication, which was outside core Postgres and not available on 9.2.
tradeoffs.why: Uber's problems came from physical replication and from every index pointing at a row's location, which no workaround removed. MySQL's logical log and primary-key indexes cut write and replication volume and made upgrades possible without rebuilding every replica, in exchange for slower reads through secondary indexes and more complex memory management.

digest.failures: During a routine primary promotion, a bug in some 9.2 releases made replicas follow the log incorrectly, so rows that should have been dead stayed visible and queries returned duplicates. Because replication was physical, the damage was in every replica's files, and Uber had to rebuild them from a fresh snapshot a few at a time. Archiving the log fell behind at peak, and the one major upgrade Uber completed, 9.1 to 9.2, took so long it could not repeat it.
digest.takeaways: A write-ahead log is what makes a database recoverable, and how you ship it decides what replicas can do: physical replication copies disk pages and inherits every bug and layout detail, while logical replication copies row changes and lets versions differ. Every index is another write on every update. Treat this as the 2016 picture; later versions may behave differently.

digest.problem: MySQL 5.7 was nearing the end of its support, so GitHub had to move its whole MySQL fleet to 8.0 without breaking its service level objectives, and with a way back at every step. This is the operational view: how a fleet of primaries, replicas and replication streams is actually run and changed at scale.
digest.constraints: The fleet has over 1,200 hosts on Azure virtual machines and GitHub's own hardware, holding over 300 TB across more than 50 clusters, each a primary with replicas, split by product area and, for the largest, sharded with Vitess. Each cluster had to be upgraded as one unit, mixed versions had to run for a long time, and a rollback had to be possible without disruption. MySQL officially supports replicating only to the next newer release, so replicating from 8.0 back to 5.7 was outside what it promises.

walkthrough.explanation: 8.0 ran in CI next to 5.7, tooling learned the syntax differences, and character sets and client settings were standardized so data could still replicate back to 5.7.
One replica was upgraded and watched, then data center by data center, always keeping enough 5.7 replicas to roll back.
Once 8.0 replicas served all reads, traffic to the 5.7 replicas stopped.
An 8.0 replica became the next primary. Below it ran a chain of 8.0 replicas serving traffic and an idle chain of 5.7 replicas, kept current by replicating backwards.
orchestrator moved the primary role to 8.0, and was told never to promote a 5.7 host, so an unplanned failover could not silently roll back.

walkthrough.step: Wait a full day, then clean up
walkthrough.explanation: 5.7 hosts stayed until at least one full 24-hour traffic cycle, peak included, passed on 8.0.
A tool called freno slowed writes when replicas lagged, and Vitess was told per keyspace when to report version 8.0 to clients.

tradeoffs.chosen: Upgrade replicas first, move reads, fail over the primary gracefully, and keep 5.7 replicas fed by backward replication until a full day of traffic passed.
tradeoffs.rejected: Upgrading primaries in place, and adopting 8.0's newer default character set, which 5.7 could not replicate.
tradeoffs.why: Every step had to be reversible, and replication was the only practical way back. That meant spare capacity for idle 5.7 hosts, an older character set for a while, and a long, cluster-by-cluster schedule.

digest.failures: In staging, promoting an 8.0 primary broke replication to every 5.7 replica, because of the character set and of permission statements 5.7 could not apply. A MySQL bug could hang replicas under heavy load until 8.0.28 fixed it. On clusters with many different clients, backward replication broke within hours, shrinking the rollback window. Queries with tens of thousands of values in a WHERE IN list passed CI but crashed MySQL in production, and replication lag under write bursts was worse on 8.0.
digest.takeaways: Replication is not only for reads and failover; it is also how a fleet is upgraded and rolled back. Plan the way back first, upgrade the least risky copies first, and keep old copies alive until real traffic, including peak, has run on the new version.

comparison: Read together, the two posts are how a database works and how one is run at scale. Uber's 2016 account explains the machinery: a write-ahead log, indexes that point at row locations, and Postgres 9.2 shipping that log to replicas as physical disk changes, which tied every replica to the primary's version and spread a bug to all of them. GitHub's 2023 post shows the operational side: MySQL replicas apply a log of row or statement changes rather than disk pages, and GitHub relied on replicating that log, even backwards from 8.0 to 5.7, to run both versions side by side and keep a path back, though that broke within hours on some clusters. The common thread is that the replication log decides how freely you can upgrade, recover and roll back.

glossary.definition: The database server that accepts writes for a dataset.
A copy of the primary that applies its log, usually serving reads and standing by to take over.
A log of every change, written before the data files are touched, so the database can recover after a crash.
The point where a transaction's log record is safely stored, after which the change must survive a crash.
MySQL's record of committed changes, as statements or rows, which replicas apply.
Shipping changes to disk pages versus shipping changes to rows; logical replication lets replicas differ in version and layout.
Multi-version concurrency control: keeping old row versions so readers see a consistent snapshot while writers continue.

mistakes: Adding indexes as if they were free. Every index is another write on every update, and in the Postgres version Uber described, an update touched every index on the table.
Holding a transaction open while doing unrelated work, such as calling another service. In Uber's account this tied up connections on the primary and could get queries on replicas cancelled.
Starting a major version upgrade without a way back. GitHub kept old-version replicas fed by backward replication; without that, an upgrade is a one-way door.

why.outcome: After this you can explain what a database guarantees that a plain file does not.
why.body:
A server keeps working data in memory, which is fast but lost in a crash, and on disk, which survives but is slower. Many clients also read and change the same data at once. Without care, a crash halfway through a change leaves data half written, and two clients can overwrite each other.

A database exists to make that safe. Once it says a change is committed, the change survives a crash, and every client sees a consistent picture. Almost every other topic here, from replication to caching to sharding, is built on top of how a database does this.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture what happens between a write and a crash-safe commit.
mentalModel.body:
Think of a database as a ledger with a diary. Before changing any data file, it writes what it is about to do in the diary, the write-ahead log. A commit is the moment that log record is safely on disk. The data files can be updated later, at leisure.

If the machine crashes, the database reads the log on restart and redoes committed changes and undoes the rest. Copies on other machines, replicas, stay current the same way: they replay the primary's log, in the same order.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through a write, a crash recovery and how replicas follow.

steps.explanation: A change to a row, and to every index that points at it, is appended to the write-ahead log.
The log record is flushed to disk. From now on the change survives a crash.
Pages in memory are written to the data files in the background.
On restart the database replays the log, redoing committed work and rolling back work that never committed.
Replicas receive the log and apply it. Physical replication ships disk-level changes; logical replication ships row or statement changes and lets each replica work out its own files.
Each index is another structure to update, and log, on every write that touches it.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace how a database's internals shaped real decisions at two companies.

steps.explanation: In a 2016 post about Postgres 9.2, Uber showed that updating one row wrote a new row version at a new location, so every index needed a new entry, at least 4 physical writes in its small example table.
Postgres 9.2 shipped its log as disk changes, so each replica was a byte-for-byte copy. When a 9.2 bug corrupted replicas, the damage was in every copy's files and they had to be rebuilt.
MySQL's binary log ships row or statement changes, so replicas work out their own index updates and can run a different version.
In 2023 GitHub upgraded over 1,200 MySQL hosts from 5.7 to 8.0 by upgrading replicas first and moving reads to them.
After failing the primary over to 8.0, GitHub kept 5.7 replicas fed by replicating backwards, and removed them only after a full 24-hour traffic cycle.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid the three most common database mistakes.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: When is a change committed?
options: When its log record is safely on disk
When the data file is updated
quiz.why: The write-ahead log is what recovery uses, so a durable log record is what makes the change safe.
wrong: Data files are updated later; the log already makes the change safe.
A commit on the primary does not wait for replicas unless configured to.

quiz.question: A database crashes after committing a change but before updating its data files. What happens on restart?
options: It replays the log and the change is applied
quiz.why: Recovery redoes every committed change found in the log.
wrong: The log record survived, so the change is redone.
Recovery is exactly what the log is for.

quiz.question: Why does adding an index slow down writes?
options: Every index is another structure to update and log on each write
Indexes are stored on replicas only
quiz.why: An index speeds some reads but adds work to every write that touches it.
wrong: Indexes do not lock the table by themselves.
Indexes live on the primary as well.

quiz.question: What does physical replication ship to replicas?
options: Disk-level changes, so replicas are byte-for-byte copies
quiz.why: That ties replicas to the primary's version and layout, including its bugs.
wrong: That is closer to logical replication.

quiz.question: Why do databases write a log before touching data files?
options: So a crash midway can be repaired from the log
Because logs are smaller than data
quiz.why: Memory is lost in a crash; the log records what to redo or undo.
wrong: The log is about safety, not read speed.

quiz.question: How did GitHub keep a way back while upgrading MySQL?
options: Old-version replicas kept receiving changes by replicating backwards from the new primary
It took full backups and planned to restore
It upgraded every host at once
quiz.why: Replication, not backups, was the practical rollback path.
wrong: A restore would lose recent writes and take hours.
That would leave no way back.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how a database works underneath and how one is upgraded at scale.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain how the replication log decides how freely you can upgrade and recover.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a slow table, design an upgrade, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: Writes to a busy table got slower after the team added six indexes for new reports. What do you check and change?
exercises.answer: Check which indexes are actually used. Every index is another write and log record on each update, so drop unused ones and serve heavy reports from a replica.
exercises.tradeoffs: Fewer indexes make some reads slower; reports on a replica see slightly old data.
wrongAnswers: Adding more indexes to speed up the writes.

exercises.prompt: Plan a major-version upgrade of a database cluster with a primary and several replicas, with a way back at every step.
exercises.answer: Test the new version in CI, upgrade one replica and watch it, then upgrade replicas in batches while keeping enough old ones. Move reads, fail over the primary gracefully, and keep old-version replicas fed by replicating backwards until a full day of traffic, peak included, has passed.
exercises.tradeoffs: Spare capacity for idle old replicas, older settings for a while, and a long schedule.
wrongAnswers: Upgrading the primary in place first.
Removing old replicas before peak traffic has run on the new version.

exercises.prompt: The fleet grows from 5 clusters to 50. What has to change in how you run upgrades?
exercises.answer: Automate each step, upgrade cluster by cluster, throttle writes when replicas lag, and expect long periods of mixed versions, so every tool must handle both.
exercises.tradeoffs: Automation takes time to build; mixed versions mean testing twice.
wrongAnswers: Doing upgrades by hand per cluster.
Assuming all clusters behave the same.
Planning for a short mixed-version window.

next.body: Replicas replay the primary's log, but that raises new questions: how many copies must hold a change before it counts, and who takes over when the primary fails. Replication picks up from there.
